title: Should R.cache be moved from Suggests to Imports?
description:
Problems with R.cache: 
- The user has to allow R.cache to create a permanent cache once, no matter whether the package is in Suggests or Imports.
- For non-interactive use (e.g. via lorenzwalthert/precommit, via REditorSupport/languageserver), the information to be displayed to the user about authorising R.cache to create such a permanent directory once is suppressed, so all these users will only benefit from caching within the a session. For pre-commit, this is never, because the hook runs in an isolated session.

Solution to R.cache problems: Provide detailed installation instructions in the README,  on the command line and to maintainers of downstream dependencies like REditorSupport/languageserver or lorenzwalthert/precommit so they inform their users about this.

Problem with Suggests:

- People will be prompted after upgrading styler to install the package `R.cache` manually.

Advantages with Suggest:

- for a lightweight use of styler, for example as part of CI/CD, the recursive dependencies of `R.cache` can be omitted. The diff is: `R.methodsS3 (>= 1.7.1), R.oo (>= 1.23.0), R.utils (>=\n2.8.0), digest (>= 0.6.13)`. Con: In CI/CD, you also want to use caching, so no one cares about these extra dependencies because the quicker styling will make up for the longer installation times.

- Potentially, when CRAN limits the max number of direct dependencies, we'd have one less if the limit is on `Imports:`.

@krlmlr what do you think? Alternatively, we can leave it in suggests and return an error if `R.cache` is not installed and say "install it to use caching" and provide a way to silence this error.

title: R devel operator precedence fix makes styler fail on CRAN
description:
From R core:

> the R parser changed in 77722 (PR#16710), fixing the precedence of "?" with respect to "=" to be as documented (lower) and as it seems it was until 2001. The change affects these packages, which will start failing their tests now [...]

The diff is here: https://github.com/wch/r-source/commit/84bbf385f909c0223924c310af6c7c77aa810234

The change is that the token `eq_assign` was renamed to `expr_or_assign_or_help` in certain situations:

```r
# R 3.6
> getParseData(parse(text = "a = 2"), includeText = TRUE)
  line1 col1 line2 col2 id parent        token terminal  text
8     1    1     1    5  8      0 equal_assign    FALSE a = 2
1     1    1     1    1  1      3       SYMBOL     TRUE     a
3     1    1     1    1  3      8         expr    FALSE     a
2     1    3     1    3  2      8    EQ_ASSIGN     TRUE     =
4     1    5     1    5  4      5    NUM_CONST     TRUE     2
5     1    5     1    5  5      8         expr    FALSE     2
```


```r
# R devel
  line1 col1 line2 col2 id parent                  token terminal text
9     1    1     1    5  9      0 expr_or_assign_or_help    FALSE     
1     1    1     1    1  1      3                 SYMBOL     TRUE    a
3     1    1     1    1  3      9                   expr    FALSE     
2     1    3     1    3  2      9              EQ_ASSIGN     TRUE    =
5     1    5     1    5  5      6              NUM_CONST     TRUE    2
6     1    5     1    5  6      9                   expr    FALSE     
```

This means `parser_version_find()` is fooled into believing that the code origins from parser version 1, but it comes from 2 (or should we even name it 3?)

This will change the structure of the parse data because the equal assign will be relocated, adding another intermediate *nest*.

Solution: set the parser version to 3 and document it.

title: Add styler pre-commit hook
description: style styler with styler. On every commit.

title: FATAL: styler's caching feature removes code
description:
We strongly discourage to use the caching feature for now. You can `cache_deactivate()` or simply get the latest GitHub version which will soon deactivate the cache by default.
Investingation ongoing. Reference: https://github.com/krlmlr/dm/issues/267.

The problems are now better understood. There are two cases:

- Uncomment roxgen code examples. When the content of roxygen code examples was cached and is multi-line, it may have contained the newline character `\n`, because we  use `text` of these tokens. When we masked the roxygen comment with `#'`, the newlines got evaluated only afterwards, adding new line breaks.

- Deleting comments: Comments can have parent 0 or negative, depending on what other tokens are present. We dropped these tokens in `drop_cached_children()` when they had negative parents after a cached expression because they would end up in the same block as the expression before it and `find_pos_id_to_keep()` only keeps the first token (which is a top-level token, form which we take `text`) and hence discards the other tokens.

title: Cache on expression level
description:
Smart caching would be done by top level expressions, i.e. cache every top level expression separately (but process all non-cached top-level expressions as a block since we need to run all styling separately on them otherwise).  The current implementation only helps when styling files that are already styled, e.g. it will make `style_pkg()` considerably faster if most files are already styled previously. It will also make the styler pre-commit hook run faster. However, when changing one line in a big file that was styled previously, the cache for all expressions is invalidated and there is no benefit from caching. 

There is stale WIP at https://github.com/lorenzwalthert/styler/tree/caching-top-level-expr.

title: T and TRUE / F and FALSE
description:
The [Introduction to R](https://cran.r-project.org/doc/manuals/r-release/R-intro.html#Logical-vectors) states in section 2.4 that you should not use the abbreviations `T` and `F` for `TRUE` and `FALSE` since `T` and `F` are just variables that are set to `TRUE` and `FALSE` by default but can be overwritten by the user. 

The [tidyverse style guide](http://style.tidyverse.org/syntax.html#object-names), does not explicitly discourage the use of `T` and `F`, but always uses `TRUE` and `FALSE` as the logical values.

As of 00f0d96, styler does not convert the values `T` and `F` to `TRUE` and `FALSE`. Since `T` and `F` might have been assigned other values than the default, such a conversion would be highly problematic.
On the other hand, currently, `T` and `F` are just left as is, without message to the user, which is probably also not the thing we would expect from styler. 

To conclude, checking for the usage of `T` and `F` and return a warning might be a reasonable way to go, so the user can resolve the problem manually.

title: Cache parse data without text
description:
Experimental idea: A smart cache would not consider `text` in it's hash function, which would allow it to discover code that matches a style but has different text. For example: 

``` r
library(magrittr)

relevant_pd_cols <- c(
  # "line1", "col1", "line2", "col2", 
  "id", "parent", "token"
  )

drop_src <- function(x) {
  all <- attributes(x)
  all$srcfile <- NULL
  attributes(x) <- all
  x
}

styler:::get_parse_data("121 + 1")[, relevant_pd_cols] %>%
  drop_src() %>%
  digest::digest()
#> [1] "96b8edf539e48f141dde75519411be06"


styler:::get_parse_data("2 + 1")[,relevant_pd_cols] %>%
  drop_src() %>%
  digest::digest()
#> [1] "96b8edf539e48f141dde75519411be06"
```

<sup>Created on 2020-01-13 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v0.3.0)</sup>

A cache based on this hash function does not work with the current implementation of the caching (which caches correct styling), but rather cache *inputs* instead of *outputs*. But also not really, because if we don't know if the text is different, how could we ever use a cached value?

title: Pretty-printting of function call in Usage section in .Rd
description:
Rendered help files for multi-line function calls have a `Usage` section that look like the one (taken from for `dplyr::join()`):
```r
# S3 method for class 'tbl_df'
inner_join(x, y, by = NULL, copy = FALSE,
  suffix = c(".x", ".y"), ...,
  na_matches = pkgconfig::get_config("dplyr::na_matches"))
```

I think developers should potentially have control over how their `Usage` section is printed. In particular, to make it compliant with their style guide of choice. As the primary style guide supported by styler is the tidyverse style guide, this should rather look like this:

```r
# S3 method for class 'tbl_df'
inner_join(x, y,
  by = NULL, copy = FALSE,
  suffix = c(".x", ".y"), ...,
  na_matches = pkgconfig::get_config("dplyr::na_matches")
)
```

Manually changing the `.Rd` source and re-building a package, I noted that line breaks in `\usage{}` are respected, which means we could in principle apply an arbitrary style guide to the code before writing to the `.Rd`. In other words, styler could be used to tidy up the code. We could let users opt-in for the tidyverse compliant styling via the roxygen field in `DESCRIPTION` that is already used for other options. 

```r
Roxygen: list(
      markdown = TRUE, 
      roclets =  c("rd", "namespace", "collate", "pkgapi::api_roclet", "styler::style_usage_roclet")
)
```


@krlmlr implemented https://github.com/r-lib/pkgapi that uses this field. Maybe you @krlmlr could support us develop this feature as you are already experienced with this? Should be a quick shot. Alternatively, this feature could be implemented in roxygen itself. Don't know what the best place is, happy to discuss.


Also, for this to not end in a one-line formatting, we potentially need styler to be able to break long lines (as WIP at #390 ) if roxygen does not handle that before with the `rd` roclet.


On a related note: We recently implemented styling of roxygen example code source in https://github.com/r-lib/styler/pull/381.

```r
styler::style_text("my_df %>% group_by(var1, var2, var3) %>% summarise(a = mean(value), b = median(value), c = sum(value)) %>% filter(a > 2, b < 1)")
```

leads to 
```r
my_df %>% group_by(var1, var2, var3) %>% summarise(a = mean(value), b = median(value), c = sum(value)) %>% filter(a > 2, b < 1)
```
and not something like
```r
my_df %>%
  group_by(var1, var2, var3) %>%
  summarise(a = mean(value), b = median(value)) %>%
  filter(a > 2, b < 1)
```

So pipes are not followed by a line break. I looked at http://styler.r-lib.org/articles/introducing_styler.html and https://lorenzwalthert.netlify.com/post/customizing-styler-the-quick-way/ how the tidyverse default style is being applied, and I don't see anything resembling the proposed style on https://style.tidyverse.org/pipes.html#whitespace:
```r
# Good
iris %>%
  group_by(Species) %>%
  summarize_if(is.numeric, mean) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  gather(measure, value, -Species) %>%
  arrange(value)

# Bad
iris %>% group_by(Species) %>% summarize_all(mean) %>%
ungroup %>% gather(measure, value, -Species) %>%
arrange(value)
```

Isn't or shouldn't this be the default behaviour of `styler::tidyverse_style()`?? Can I change this behaviour?

title: R CMD CHECK ERROR on r-devel-linux-x86_64-debian-clang
description:
Most likely due to the charset changed from UTF-8 to ISO8859-15 and special characters printed with the cli packge, which does [not fail](https://cran.r-project.org/web/checks/check_results_cli.html) on the aforementioned flavor. 
Seems to appear in other repos also, e.g. [pillar](https://cran.r-project.org/web/checks/check_results_pillar.html) and was discussed on [r-devel](https://stat.ethz.ch/pipermail/r-package-devel/2019q2/003755.html), but I don't know which conclusions to draw from it. One potential fix is to skip tests on CRAN if the encoding is not UTF8, but this seems not an ideal solution. It was done [here](https://github.com/davidgohel/fpeek/commit/e45d74acad073b223ac36908461a962e01efdf68) for example.

This is how the output of styler looks in case things are going well: 
![Screen Shot 2019-04-25 at 22 57 39](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/10477073/56768036-8a5f1100-67ad-11e9-8c9e-4e16f714f943.png)

I don't know how to fix this. We are required to submit a new version of styler to CRAN for other reasons, namely #490, until May 10, so I thought we could fix this as well until then (if we knew how). 

cc: @krlmlr, @gaborcsardi, @davidgohel.

description:

description:
Because of a typo in the source code (`text` instead of `texts`), styler returns an error when `length(text)` does not return 1.
``` r

)
styler::style_text(text)
#> Error: pd must be a wrapped expression that has one row.
```

title: Upcoming fix in R devel parser requires action
description:
```r
> getParseData(parse(text = "t = 1")) 
# current R 3.5.1
  line1 col1 line2 col2 id parent     token terminal text
1     1    1     1    1  1      3    SYMBOL     TRUE    t
3     1    1     1    1  3      0      expr    FALSE
2     1    2     1    2  2      0 EQ_ASSIGN     TRUE    =
4     1    3     1    3  4      5 NUM_CONST     TRUE    1
5     1    3     1    3  5      0      expr    FALSE

# R devel after committed by Tomas Kalibera
  line1 col1 line2 col2 id parent        token terminal text
8     1    1     1    3  8      0 equal_assign    FALSE <==== I added this
1     1    1     1    1  1      3       SYMBOL     TRUE    t
3     1    1     1    1  3      8         expr    FALSE
2     1    2     1    2  2      8    EQ_ASSIGN     TRUE    =
4     1    3     1    3  4      5    NUM_CONST     TRUE    1
5     1    3     1    3  5      8         expr    FALSE
```

Note the new token, which is *not* an `expr` and that all ids are changed. I was notified by the creator of the bug fix Tomas Kalibera as this will cause `R CMD CHECK` of styler (and reverse dependencies) to fail on R devel.

I see the following solution: Nest the parse data as is. Then, don't relocate the `EQ_ASSIGN` if a token `equal_assign` is present in a nest.
```r
relocate_eq_assign <- function(pd) {
  if (any(pd$token == "equal_assign")) {
    pd
  } else {
    pd %>%
      post_visit(c(relocate_eq_assign_nest))
  }
}
```
@krlmlr what do you think should we do? Should we wait until the bug fix of the base R parser is implemented in R devel, fix the problem here and create a new release? I think I can't guarantee that this works and submit before the changes are implemented in R devel and I won't build R devel myself.

title: Switch to error handling with rlang
description:
Reason: it seems as it raises *nicer* error messages (no `Error in value[[3L]](cond)`)  and does not need to re-throw explicitly plus other reasons mentioned in https://www.tidyverse.org/articles/2018/10/rlang-0-3-0/. 
``` r

result <- tryCatch(stop("x is not good"),
  error = function(e) stop("The error message is:", conditionMessage(e))
)
#> Error in value[[3L]](cond): The error message is:x is not good
library(rlang)
#> Warning: package 'rlang' was built under R version 3.5.2

with_handlers(abort("x is not good"),
  error = ~ abort(paste("error x: THe error message is:", .$message))
)
#> Error: error x: THe error message is: x is not good
```

<sup>Created on 2019-02-17 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v0.2.1)</sup>

Less concise alternative with base R that gives desired result: 
``` r

result <- tryCatch(stop("x is not good"),
  error = function(e) e
)
if (inherits(result, "error")) {
  stop("error x: The error message is:", result$message, call. = FALSE)
}
#> Error: error x: The error message is:x is not good
```

title: styling with `scope = "spaces"` yields wrong indention for roxygen code example
description:
``` r
styler::style_text("\n#' There\n#' @examples\n#' if (TRUE) {\n#'  return(x1)\n#'}\nx <- y\n",
  scope = "spaces"
)
#> 
#> #' There
#> #' @examples
#> #' if (TRUE) {
#> #' return(x1)
#> #' }
#> x <- y
```

<sup>Created on 2019-01-04 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v0.2.1)</sup>

The `return()` statement should remain indented by two spaces. The problem does not occur when the code is not roxygen code example code: 

``` r
styler::style_text("\nif (TRUE) {\n return(x1)\n}\nx <- y\n",
  scope = "spaces"
)
#> 
#> if (TRUE) {
#>  return(x1)
#> }
#> x <- y
```

 ``` r
styler::style_text("\n#' There\n#' @examples\nif (TRUE) {\n return(x1)\n}\nx <- y\n")

description:

Noticed this bug [when running `style_pkg()` today](https://github.com/ropensci/monkeylearn/commit/0bb57e918abcf5f234249fe28f027a09dd89d8cd) but reproduced using `style_file()` on the following text. room of technologically inclined students was that Wall Street was where they could find far more challenging,
diverse and, yes, lucrative jobs working on some of the worlds most difficult technical problems.\n\n 
Whereas in other opportunities you might be considering, it is working one type of data or one type of

title: Making most important programming conventions explicit in CONTRIBUTING
description:
With regard to GSOC 2018, but also with regard to other contributors to the source code of styler, it might be worth trying to put the most important conventions into the file CONTRIBUTING so new contributors don't have a hard time embracing them. This is likely to avoid frictions in the code base that future contributions might expose. Since these conventions are not supposed to change in the future, the maintenance effort remains minimal. Examples would be: 

* The tidyverse style guide is used.
* vectors holding boolean values have a name which corresponds to a question that can be answered with yes or no. Perfix `is` or `has` is common. Example: `is_larger_than_reference`.
* Vectors holding indices are suffixed with `idx`.

title: Adding roundtrip for nested processing
description:
Might be implemented similar to depreciated flat roundtrip
```r
#' Verify parse data modifications
#'
#' @description Check whether serializing the parse data results in the same
#' number of lines as the initial data that should be styled.
#' @param pd_flat A parse table.
#' @param text A character vector with the initial text to compare against.
#' @return If the verification is successful, `pd` is returned, with empty
#'   lines at the end of `text` stripped. \cr
#'   Otherwise, an error is thrown.
#' @seealso [serialize_parse_data_flat()]
verify_roundtrip <- function(pd_flat, text) {
  roundtrip <- serialize_parse_data_flat(pd_flat)

  if (length(roundtrip) < length(text)) {
    stopifnot(text[-seq_along(roundtrip)] == "")
    text <- text[seq_along(roundtrip)]
  }

  stopifnot(identical(text, roundtrip))
  text
}
```

title: Verify lossless parse + serialize (without transforms)
description:
A run without any transformers enabled should yield exactly the same results as the input, minus spaces at EOL and conversion of tabs to spaces. This should be tested separately on all input files, for easier isolation of parse/serialize problems from transformer problems during later refactorings.

Since the initial release of styler, some important bugs were fixed:

title: Renaming
description:
# Naming of data
At the moment, for the parse table returned by utils::getParseData and 
processed through various functions, we use many different names in different 
functions for essentially this (flat) table:

* pd (all rules in rules.R)
* parse_data (serialize_parse_data)
* parse_data_with_ws (serialize_parse_data_flat)
* data (create_filler)

I think it would simplify things to just use one variable name throughout. I
suggest parse_data. We could use `parse_data_flt` for the flat version and and 
`parse_data_nstd` for the nested version for situations where the processing
differs.

# Naming of functions
As far as I understand, the terminology around `ws` is more of a legacy thing, i.e. in the functions `compute_parse_data_flat_with_ws` or `add_ws_to_parse_data` since it is not really just white space information that is affected by these functions, but rather a bunch of preprocessing Hence, I would suggest to rename the latter to `pre_process_parse_data` and the former to `compute_parse_data_flt` for now.

}

title: Multiline function arguments
description:
``` r
styler::style_text("with(\na = 1,\n{\ncode\n}\n)", strict = FALSE, scope = "line_breaks")
#> with(
#>   a = 1, {
#>     code
#>   }
#> )
```

The opening brace should stay on its own line, we should also insert a line break if there is none.

``` r
styler::style_text("with(a = 1,\n{\ncode\n})", strict = FALSE, scope = "line_breaks")
#> with(a = 1, {
#>   code
#> })
```

The `test_that()` calls should be an exception: We allow this if the code argument is the last one and all other arguments start on the same line as the argument

``` r
styler::style_text("call({\ncode\n},\narg1 = FALSE)", strict = FALSE, scope = "line_breaks")
#> call({
#>   code
#> },
#> arg1 = FALSE)
```

In this case, I think we should add a line break after the opening paren even for `strict = FALSE`, unless the code block is the only argument.

``` r
styler::style_text("structure(list(\na=1), class=)")
#> structure(list(
#>   a = 1
#> ), class = )
```

Essentially the same as above. (And we never continue after a multi-line argument, the `class =` goes on its own line.)

title: style_file() unexpectedly deletes non-ASCII characters on Windows
description:
(Sorry, this is a "manual" reprex, as it throws errors on reading/writing to the tempfile.)

```r
tmp <- tempfile(fileext = ".R")

con <- file(tmp, encoding = "UTF-8")

# "1+1" needs spaces
writeLines("# 忍者\n1+1", con)

readLines(con)
#> [1] "# 忍者" "1+1"

styler::style_file(tmp)

#> ----------------------------------------
#> Status	Count	Legend 
#> √ 	0	File unchanged.
#> i 	1	File changed.
#> x 	0	Styling threw an eror.
#> ----------------------------------------
#> Please review the changes carefully!


# the comment "# 忍者" disappeared...
readLines(con)
# [1] ""      "1 + 1"
```

I think the root cause is this line in enc package; `from = "UTF-8"` should not set here as it seems that text is encoded as the default encoding.

https://github.com/krlmlr/enc/blob/883df89f77bb5f8646b9a8fa94cc72120cdf0c81/R/io.R#L59

title: Line breaks and named arguments
description:
Line breaks should not be forced after the opening brace of a function call if the call follows a structure like
```r
map(x, c, 
  furher_arg = 3,
  another_arg = 2:4
)
```
Reference: https://github.com/tidyverse/style/issues/39

Hence, when modifying line breaks after `(`, one has to check the structure and only break the line before the first named argument.
More concretely, 
* if expression is a function call,
* and expression spans over multiple lines
* find the first named argument and add a line break before it.
* If no named argument occurs (but there is at least one argument), break after opening brace.

description:

Input file:

    code_block(
      paste0("#' @useDynLib ", project_name(), ", .registration = TRUE"),
      "#' @importFrom Rcpp sourceCpp",
      "NULL"
    )
  } else {
    todo("Include the following directives in your NAMESPACE")

      paste0("useDynLib('", project_name(), "', .registration = TRUE)"),

```

Output using "Style active file" addin:

``` r

#'
#' @inheritParams use_template
#' @export
use_rcpp <- function() {
  use_dependency("Rcpp", "LinkingTo")
  use_dependency("Rcpp", "Imports")
  
  use_directory("src")
  use_git_ignore(c("*.o", "*.so", "*.dll"), "src")

    todo("Include the following directives in your NAMESPACE")

      paste0("useDynLib('", project_name(), "', .registration = TRUE)"),

title: rplumber support
description:
styler breaks `rplumber` syntax by inserting a space between `#` and `*`. E.g. take the following example from www.rplumber.io.
```r
# myfile.R

#* @get /mean
normalMean <- function(samples=10){
  data <- rnorm(samples)
  mean(data)
}

#* @post /sum
addTwo <- function(a, b){
  as.numeric(a) + as.numeric(b)
}
```
This won't work anymore with `# * @get ` etc. 

It seems as all plumber tags are listed [here](https://www.rplumber.io/docs/routing-and-input.html#endpoints). The list includes

* `@get`
* `@post`
* `@put`
* `@delete`
* `@head`

I think we simply may adapt the regex pattern in https://github.com/r-lib/styler/blob/master/R/rules-spacing.R#L189 to not only support `#'`, but also `#*`. I don't see any conflicts since roxygen markdown syntax uses `#' * bullet` (so it won't match).

cc: @trestletech

title: allow rmd styling also via style_dir() and style_pkg()
description:
`style_dir()` and `style_pkg()` should gain a new argument `extension` (that defaults to `c("R")`) to indicate which types of extensions should be styled. It should handle:
* just R files (`extension = "R"` or `extension = c("R")`).
* just Rmd files (`extension = "Rmd"` or `extension = c("Rmd")`).
* both (`extension = c("Rmd", "R")`).

The case should be ignored, i.e. `extension = c("rMd")` should be accepted. Nice to have: a trailing dot is removed (i.e. `extension = c(".Rmd")` also works).

title: Function declarations
description:
``` r
styler::style_text("function (a = 1,\nb = 2\n){\nNULL\n}", strict = FALSE, scope = "indention")
#> function (a = 1,
#>          b = 2
#>        ) {
#>   NULL
#> }
```

title: inconsistency in getParseData?
description:
Why is the following different and what can we do about it?

``` r
arrow <- "a <- 3"
eq <- "a = 3"

styler:::create_tree(arrow)
#>                                             levelName
#> 1 ROOT (token: short_text [lag_newlines/spaces] {id})
#> 2  °--expr:  [0/0] {7}                               
#> 3      ¦--expr:  [0/1] {3}                           
#> 4      ¦   °--SYMBOL: a [0/0] {1}                    
#> 5      ¦--LEFT_ASSIGN: <- [0/1] {2}                  
#> 6      °--expr:  [0/0] {5}                           
#> 7          °--NUM_CONST: 3 [0/0] {4}
styler:::create_tree(eq)
#>                                             levelName
#> 1 ROOT (token: short_text [lag_newlines/spaces] {id})
#> 2  ¦--expr:  [0/1] {3}                               
#> 3  ¦   °--SYMBOL: a [0/0] {1}                        
#> 4  ¦--EQ_ASSIGN: = [0/1] {2}                         
#> 5  °--expr:  [0/0] {5}                               
#> 6      °--NUM_CONST: 3 [0/0] {4}

utils::getParseData(parse(text = eq))
#>  line1 col1 line2 col2 id parent     token terminal text
#> 1     1    1     1    1  1      3    SYMBOL     TRUE    a
#> 3     1    1     1    1  3      0      expr    FALSE     
#> 2     1    3     1    3  2      0 EQ_ASSIGN     TRUE    =
#> 4     1    5     1    5  4      5 NUM_CONST     TRUE    3
#> 5     1    5     1    5  5      0      expr    FALSE     

utils::getParseData(parse(text = arrow))
#>  line1 col1 line2 col2 id parent     token terminal text
#> 7     1    1     1    6  7      0        expr    FALSE     
#> 1     1    1     1    1  1      3      SYMBOL     TRUE    a
#> 3     1    1     1    1  3      7        expr    FALSE     
#> 2     1    3     1    4  2      7 LEFT_ASSIGN     TRUE   <-
#> 4     1    6     1    6  4      5   NUM_CONST     TRUE    3
#> 5     1    6     1    6  5      7        expr    FALSE     
```
Now there was just one expression, but the problem is worse if there are multiple, because with `=`, 
they will all be on the same level, i.e. more than one expression has parent 0.
```r
styler:::create_tree("a = 3 \n 3")
#>                                             levelName
#> 1 ROOT (token: short_text [lag_newlines/spaces] {id})
#> 2  ¦--expr:  [0/1] {3}                               
#> 3  ¦   °--SYMBOL: a [0/0] {1}                        
#> 4  ¦--EQ_ASSIGN: = [0/1] {2}                         
#> 5  ¦--expr:  [0/1] {5}                               
#> 6  ¦   °--NUM_CONST: 3 [0/0] {4}                     
#> 7  °--expr:  [1/0] {12}                              
#> 8      °--NUM_CONST: 3 [0/0] {11}

#> line1 col1 line2 col2 id parent     token terminal text
#> 1      1    1     1    1  1      3    SYMBOL     TRUE    a
#> 3      1    1     1    1  3      0      expr    FALSE     
#> 2      1    3     1    3  2      0 EQ_ASSIGN     TRUE    =
#> 4      1    5     1    5  4      5 NUM_CONST     TRUE    3
#> 5      1    5     1    5  5      0      expr    FALSE     
#> 11     2    2     2    2 11     12 NUM_CONST     TRUE    3
#> 12     2    2     2    2 12      0      expr    FALSE     
```

For us, it is a problem if we want to indent based on `=`. We can just indent the token after `=`, but 
if within that expression we have something that also needs indention, we cannot flatten out and will have too much indention:
```
a =
  b +  # still correct
    c + # not correct anymore
    d

title: Extensibility: Third-party style guide support
description:
At it’s core, a style guide is a collection of transformer functions that fulfill certain formal requirements. 
It would be nice if styler could support style guides defined by third parties. 
In the following, I lay out a potential mechanism for how such a third-party support could look like. This were my first thoughts on the topic. Maybe there are better approaches to it.

Styler could provide a function to import style guides  and save them in the local package directory of styler. People who want to create style guides could provide the transformer functions for example in a GitHub repository. The style guide that should be used to format a package’s source code (and potentially further options) could then be specified in a file in the root directory of that package (e.g. in styler.yml). Styler would then use the the information from this .yml file, source the corresponding .R files from the styler package directory and apply them (and potentially further options) to the source code to be formatted. The formal requirements of style guides had to be defined (i.e. before it can be imported). Potential requirements: Style guide must not yield an error when applied to a test source code. Transformer functions must have follow certain naming conventions, must be documented ect.  Provide detailed instructions how to create / test style guides etc.

title: Indention based on operators only checks first potential trigger
description:
Indention based on operators only checks first potential trigger.
``` r
test <- c(
  "1 + (", 
  "3", 
  ") %>%", 
  "x()"
)
cat(styler::style_text(test), sep = "\n")
#> 1 + (
#>   3
#> ) %>%
#> x()
```

`x()`  is not indented since it is only checked whether `+` causes indention (which is not the case since a multi-line expression follows and `(` will cause indention within the child). However, we need to check for all potential token that are triggers  (`+` and `%>%` here) and then indent on the first one for which we need indention.

title: implementation of breaking long function calls
description:
The [tidyverse style guide](http://style.tidyverse.org/syntax.html#long-lines) states that long function calls are not compliant with the style guide:

```r
# Good
do_something_very_complicated(
  "that",
  requires = many,
  arguments = "some of which may be long"
)

# Bad
do_something_very_complicated("that", requires, many, arguments,
                              "some of which may be long"
                              )
```

It also states that multiple arguments can remain on the same line if they are related.
```r
# Good
paste0(
  "Requirement: ", requires, "\n",
  "Result: ", result, "\n"
)

# Bad
paste0(
  "Requirement: ", requires,
  "\n", "Result: ",
  result, "\n")
```

I am not sure how to implement that and how strictly we should use it. A simple rule would be to add a line break after `(`, and leaving everything until `)` untouched in terms of line breaks and putting the closing `)` on a new line. Also, I think this should be a transformer that is only used if `strict = TRUE` since I think its one of the rules in the style guide that is not consistently obeyed by many people. @krlmlr maybe you can advise on that.

title: Indent indices for token "EQ_SUB" are different.
description:
The problem with the token "EQ_SUB" mentioned [here](https://github.com/yihui/tikzDevice/commit/d30b17e7011688c14984a6c7575c12da7075b2b8) arises because of the fact that expression "a = 3" and "b = 44" are not nested one level deeper, i.e. they are all direct sub-expressions of the root token:
``` r
styler:::create_tree("data_frame(a = 3, b = 44)")
#>                                              levelName
#> 1  ROOT (token: short_text [lag_newlines/spaces] {id})
#> 2   °--expr:  [0/0] {18}                              
#> 3       ¦--expr:  [0/0] {3}                           
#> 4       ¦   °--SYMBOL_FUNCTION_CALL: data_ [0/0] {1}  
#> 5       ¦--'(': ( [0/0] {2}                           
#> 6       ¦--SYMBOL_SUB: a [0/1] {4}                    
#> 7       ¦--EQ_SUB: = [0/1] {5}                        
#> 8       ¦--expr:  [0/0] {7}                           
#> 9       ¦   °--NUM_CONST: 3 [0/0] {6}                 
#> 10      ¦--',': , [0/1] {8}                           
#> 11      ¦--SYMBOL_SUB: b [0/1] {11}                   
#> 12      ¦--EQ_SUB: = [0/1] {12}                       
#> 13      ¦--expr:  [0/0] {14}                          
#> 14      ¦   °--NUM_CONST: 44 [0/0] {13}               
#> 15      °--')': ) [0/0] {15}
```

We used `compute_indent_indices()` so far to compute the indices that need indention. However, with all other operators such as braces or `+` `%>%`, the indention is always from the token on until the last or the penultimate token in that parse table. Here, it is only the next token, so we could go about it as follows:

```r
indent_eq_sub <- function(pd,
                          indent_by,
                          token = "EQ_SUB") {
  eq_sub <- which(pd$token == "EQ_SUB")
  if (length(eq_sub) == 0) return(pd)
  has_line_break <- which(pd$lag_newlines > 0)
  indent_indices <- intersect(eq_sub + 1, has_line_break)
  pd$indent[indent_indices] <- pd$indent[indent_indices] + indent_by
  pd
}
```

Alternatively, we had to modify `compute_indent_indices()`, which has already an argument `indent_last`. We could make that argument non-boolean and change it to `indent_up_to` and allow values "next", "penulatimate", "last".

title: Decide on the  usage of the `newlines` attribute
description:
A few rules still use `newlines`, which leads to problems since all line-break rules only modify `lag_newlines`, so `newlines` may contain outdated information. 
Also, if we want to allow non-invasive styling without indention correction, we need to set spaces only for tokens that are not at the end of a line. Otherwise, we "destroy" the indention information provided in the raw data. 
One may think we could use `dplyr::lead(pd$lag_newlines)`, which may work since to create `lag_newlines`, we only introduced one unknown value (at the top of the parse table) as this was done in the flat structure. Using `dplyr::lead(pd$lag_newlines)` in each nested structure will create one unknown value for the last token (instead of `pd$newlines(nrow(pd))`. We may loose information

We may need another visitor to update `newlines` (or update it right in the place where we update `lag_newlines`) so we can use this attribute when manipulating spacing information (i.e. making sure we do not update spacing information for the last token on a line).

title: Indention of function declarations
description:
Example:

```r
a <- function(x, y,
              z)
{
}
```

To achieve this, we could:

1. When processing `z`, memoize the ID of `x` as a reference for the indent depth (because we can't know how deep `x` will be indented)
2. After applying all transformers, convert relative indents to absolute indents with a "pre" visitor
3. Flatten the nested structure with a "post" visitor
4. In the flat structure, update the absolute indention depth of `z` with that of `x` with a lookup in the flat structure
5. Serialize

We could omit step 3 if the reference token is always at the same level in the nested structure.

title: work with text instead of token
description:
So far, all rules in R/rules.R operate on tokens, i.e. on this vector that contains tokens.
```r
op_token <- c(
  "'+'", "'-'", "'*'", "'/'", "'^'", "AND", "AND2", "EQ", "EQ_ASSIGN",
  "GE", "GT", "LE", "LEFT_ASSIGN", "LT", "NE", "OR", "OR2", "RIGHT_ASSIGN",
  "SPECIAL", "EQ_SUB", "ELSE")
```

For my PR #35, I was using the argument `op_token` in the function `indent_op()` in order to be consistent with previous work. It allows specifying all tokens that trigger indention. However, I think we should rather use text than token for two reasons:

* If people want to customise styler, they rather want to specify a text of a token (like `>=`) than spending time on figuring out what "LE", "GT" etc. stand for.
* More importantly, the token "SPECIAL" does not uniquely map to a text element, i.e. I suppose a case that is not covered by the tokens in `op_token` is declared as "SPECIAL". Hence, we can only define indention for all text elements corresponding to "SPECIAL".

How should we proceed?

title: distinguish operators
description:
I am not sure how we can distinguish signs of numbers (e.g. `-` in `-2`) from addition and subtraction.
Take this example:
`42 + -2 / 78`.
The tree structure for it looks as follows:
``` r
library("magrittr")
styler:::compute_parse_data_nested("42 + -2 / 78") %>% styler:::create_filler_nested() %>% 
  styler:::create_node_from_nested_root()
#>                                 levelName
#> 1  xxx                                   
#> 2   °--expr: 42 +  [0/0]                 
#> 3       ¦--expr: 42 [0/1]                
#> 4       ¦   °--NUM_CONST: 42 [0/0]       
#> 5       ¦--'+': + [0/1]                  
#> 6       °--expr: -2 /  [0/0]             
#> 7           ¦--expr: -2 [0/1]            
#> 8           ¦   ¦--'-': - [0/0]          
#> 9           ¦   °--expr: 2 [0/0]         
#> 10          ¦       °--NUM_CONST: 2 [0/0]
#> 11          ¦--'/': / [0/1]              
#> 12          °--expr: 78 [0/0]            
#> 13              °--NUM_CONST: 78 [0/0]
```
It looks as if +/- are located  at the top of a parse table, they are signs, otherwise, they are operators for subtraction / addition. 
Maybe we can look at a more complicated example.

``` r
library("magrittr")
styler:::compute_parse_data_nested("42 + (-2 - -3 *( 10 +1)/ 2) / -78") %>% 
  styler:::create_filler_nested() %>% styler:::create_node_from_nested_root()
#>                                                      levelName
#> 1  xxx                                                        
#> 2   °--expr: 42 +  [0/0]                                      
#> 3       ¦--expr: 42 [0/1]                                     
#> 4       ¦   °--NUM_CONST: 42 [0/0]                            
#> 5       ¦--'+': + [0/1]                                       
#> 6       °--expr: (-2 - [0/0]                                  
#> 7           ¦--expr: (-2 - [0/1]                              
#> 8           ¦   ¦--'(': ( [0/0]                               
#> 9           ¦   ¦--expr: -2 -  [0/0]                          
#> 10          ¦   ¦   ¦--expr: -2 [0/1]                         
#> 11          ¦   ¦   ¦   ¦--'-': - [0/0]                       
#> 12          ¦   ¦   ¦   °--expr: 2 [0/0]                      
#> 13          ¦   ¦   ¦       °--NUM_CONST: 2 [0/0]             
#> 14          ¦   ¦   ¦--'-': - [0/1]                           
#> 15          ¦   ¦   °--expr: -3 *( [0/0]                      
#> 16          ¦   ¦       ¦--expr: -3 *( [0/0]                  
#> 17          ¦   ¦       ¦   ¦--expr: -3 [0/1]                 
#> 18          ¦   ¦       ¦   ¦   ¦--'-': - [0/0]               
#> 19          ¦   ¦       ¦   ¦   °--expr: 3 [0/0]              
#> 20          ¦   ¦       ¦   ¦       °--NUM_CONST: 3 [0/0]     
#> 21          ¦   ¦       ¦   ¦--'*': * [0/0]                   
#> 22          ¦   ¦       ¦   °--expr: ( 10  [0/0]              
#> 23          ¦   ¦       ¦       ¦--'(': ( [0/1]               
#> 24          ¦   ¦       ¦       ¦--expr: 10 +1 [0/0]          
#> 25          ¦   ¦       ¦       ¦   ¦--expr: 10 [0/1]         
#> 26          ¦   ¦       ¦       ¦   ¦   °--NUM_CONST: 10 [0/0]
#> 27          ¦   ¦       ¦       ¦   ¦--'+': + [0/0]           
#> 28          ¦   ¦       ¦       ¦   °--expr: 1 [0/0]          
#> 29          ¦   ¦       ¦       ¦       °--NUM_CONST: 1 [0/0] 
#> 30          ¦   ¦       ¦       °--')': ) [0/0]               
#> 31          ¦   ¦       ¦--'/': / [0/1]                       
#> 32          ¦   ¦       °--expr: 2 [0/0]                      
#> 33          ¦   ¦           °--NUM_CONST: 2 [0/0]             
#> 34          ¦   °--')': ) [0/0]                               
#> 35          ¦--'/': / [0/1]                                   
#> 36          °--expr: -78 [0/0]                                
#> 37              ¦--'-': - [0/0]                               
#> 38              °--expr: 78 [0/0]                             
#> 39                  °--NUM_CONST: 78 [0/0]
```

Indeed it seems we could distinguish signs from operators that way

title: indention with multiple brackets
description:
Currently, styler adds indention for every opening bracket, which is the first problem.
``` r
library(magrittr)

test <- c("(((", "1", ")))")

styler::style_text(test) %>% cat(sep = "\n")
#> (((
#>       1
#>     )))
```
Instead of just 
```r
#> (((
#>   1
#>     )))
```
The tree looks as follows:
```r
styler:::compute_parse_data_nested(test) %>% styler:::visit(c(styler:::create_filler)) %>% 
  styler:::create_node_from_nested_root()
#>                                 levelName
#> 1  xxx                                   
#> 2   °--expr:  [0/0]                      
#> 3       ¦--'(': ( [0/0]                  
#> 4       ¦--expr:  [0/0]                  
#> 5       ¦   ¦--'(': ( [0/0]              
#> 6       ¦   ¦--expr:  [0/0]              
#> 7       ¦   ¦   ¦--'(': ( [1/0]          
#> 8       ¦   ¦   ¦--expr:  [1/0]          
#> 9       ¦   ¦   ¦   °--NUM_CONST: 1 [0/0]
#> 10      ¦   ¦   °--')': ) [0/0]          
#> 11      ¦   °--')': ) [0/0]              
#> 12      °--')': ) [0/0]
```
Second, it cannot "undo" indention when we put multiple closing brackets on one line, i.e. the last three brackets should not be indented, but this depends on what comes after the first bracket, and styler does not "look into the future" when serialising. That's why it gets it right when the brackets are on different lines.
```r
(((
      1
    )
  )
)
```

Rstudio only adds one level of indention per line, no matter how many opening brackets are there.
```r
((((((((
  1
))))))))
```
If the closing parenthesis are not on the same line, it un-indents all of them anyways:
```r
(((((
  1
)
)
)
)
)

```

I think the way to go is to remove indention whenever there is a child that also has indention and starts on the same line. I had it the other way round just now (see [here](https://github.com/lorenzwalthert/styler/commit/43981c877e4d97273a75b15ea695bb1e84308867)) which means only the first parenthesis has indention, all the subsequent "inner" parenthesis' indention was removed, but then the problem remains that the closing brackets are still indented by one level. 
The solution I suggest would involve setting the indention after the visitor, having to go through all levels of nesting  again. Alternatively, we could try to integrate it with the visitor we already have but I think that's a bad idea.

title: Formatter for nested parse data
description:
Use data.tree package.

Each node should contain `token`, `short`, `spaces` and `newlines`.

```r
#' @import data.tree
create_node_from_nested_root <- function(pd_nested) {
  n <- Node$new("xxx")
  create_node_from_nested(pd_nested, n)
  n
}

#' @importFrom purrr map2
create_node_from_nested <- function(pd_nested, parent) {
  if (is.null(pd_nested))
    return()

  node_info <-
    pd_nested %>%
    transmute(formatted = paste0(token, ": ", short, " [", newlines, "/", spaces, "]")) %>%
    .[["formatted"]]

  child_nodes <-
    node_info %>%
    map(parent$AddChild)

  map2(pd_nested$child, child_nodes, create_node_from_nested)
  return()
}
```
